Countervail
KOWN-ter-vayl
v.t. (to offset with equal force or value; to compensate for or balance out)
From Old French contrevaloir, from Latin contra, against, and valere, to be worth, have strength.

Biblical Definition

For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage.

This is Esther's carefully measured plea before King Ahasuerus, revealing Haman's plot and her own Jewish identity at the moment of greatest danger. She reasons that mere slavery, however bitter, would not have justified disturbing the king, since no enemy's price could countervail, could sufficiently offset or compensate, the damage such a loss of loyal subjects would do to the king's own interests; but wholesale destruction is a different matter entirely, one that demands his intervention. Esther's rhetoric is shrewd and courageous at once, appealing not merely to pity but to the king's own self-interest, while still placing the full weight of the crisis, her people's planned annihilation, before him without flinching. The word countervail captures the entire moral calculus of her appeal: Haman's bribe of ten thousand talents of silver (Est 3:9) could never truly balance the scales against the extermination of an entire people, and Esther's speech exposes that imbalance plainly.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from COUNTERVAIL: to be of equal value or force against; to compensate; to balance out an opposing weight or loss.

COUNTERVAIL, v.t. To act against with equal force, weight, or value.

To compensate for; to make up for by an equivalent.

Esther 7: no price could countervail the damage of her people's loss.

Part of Esther's shrewd, courageous appeal to the king.

Exposes the moral imbalance behind Haman's bribe for genocide.

Key Scripture

Est 7:4 — "For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage."

Modern Corruption

Reducing human life and dignity to a calculable economic value, as though some sufficient price could countervail the loss of a people, is precisely the moral logic Esther's speech exposes and rejects.

expand to see more

Utilitarian calculation sometimes treats human worth as a quantity that can, in principle, be countervailed by some sufficient compensating value, a logic Haman's ten-thousand-talent bribe (Est 3:9) embodies outright.

Esther's own appeal refuses this logic even while using its vocabulary: by naming that no price could countervail her people's destruction, she exposes the bribe's moral bankruptcy rather than endorsing the calculation. Human life made in God's image cannot be reduced to a balanced ledger (Gen 9:6).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French contrevaloir compounds Latin contra, against, with valere, to be strong or worth — to countervail is literally to hold equal worth or strength against an opposing force, a precise balancing of value.

expand to see more

Contra, against, and valere, to be worth, form contrevaloir.

To countervail is to hold equal value against an opposing force.

Esther applies it to the impossibility of pricing her people's lives.

Exposes the moral bankruptcy of Haman's bribe for genocide.

Human worth cannot be balanced by any economic equivalent.

Usage

"The enemy could not countervail the king's damage — no price could balance the loss."

"Part of Esther's shrewd and courageous appeal to Ahasuerus."

"Exposes the moral bankruptcy of pricing human life and destruction."
